utterances.text: From the operators we received information that they would receive empty notebooks, marked by the registration number and date, and then they used those notebooks to transcribe intercepted conversations. Did you receive the same information about that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In a number of notebooks, entries of intercepted conversations and the dates of intercepted conversations precede the registration number and the date of the opening of the notebook. Did you pay any heed to that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm going to object to my colleague's question to the extent that I don't believe it accurately reflects the records of these proceedings and if he has specific information with respect to when the notebooks were written in, as opposed to the date of their opening, then I would ask that he come forward with that and put that to the witness specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I think Mr. Vanderpuye's perfectly right. You need to be more specific in this, not vague or generic as you have been. So if you have a specific instance, which I'm sure you would have, go straight there, but ...

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I recall that we had some 20 witnesses, and my questions were aimed at this and they responded to that. I have to admit that I have not prepared a transcript of these testimonies, but if this is a pre-condition for my question, given that nobody in the courtroom recalls my question and the answers that we received, then I will not insist on that and I will go on to another question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's up to you, but you can rephrase your question, putting to the witness that several intercept operators have stated this, what you maintain they have stated, and then ask her whether she is -- she was aware of this, whether she's ever taken it into consideration in her analysis, had in the sense of whether it was an important factor for analysis purposes or not. But that's about it, if you want to pursue the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It seems to me that I put this question in the same way or a similar way that the witness discussed this matter of registration number and the date of registration, but -- well, I will of course follow this line and I will ask the witness whether she received, with operators with whom she conferred, information about receiving empty notebooks from the command with -- only bearing the markings of the registration number and the date of registration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think she has answered -- answered that already. She told you, "Yes, that's what they told me."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My next question. Did she notice that in certain notebooks one can -- could find entries that precede the dates of the notebook being registered with the command?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall that off the top of my head. But I would have to look at the -- at the list of registration numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could I now look at Prosecutor's Exhibit -- please bear with me just a moment. 1072 is the number of the Prosecutor's exhibit. Can we please look at enclosure number 2, and the page number is 01085070. Could you please look under number 4. The date when the notebook was opened, I mean the registration of the notebook, was it the 28th of May, 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what is indicated on this list, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, and then in the brackets, does it say that the first entry in the notebook is dated 13 of April, i.e. a month before that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Isn't the situation very similar with the following notebook on the number 5, it was registered on the 24th of April, and the first entry is dated the 10th of April?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Isn't the situation the same with notebook under number 10, which was open on the 28th of April and the first entry was made on the 4th of April, apparently?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Notebook number 11.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is this: We could go on and look at the list and find a number of such notebooks but in order to avoid wasting time, let me ask you this: Did you notice this before, and did you take this into account when you analysed and assessed the reliability of the contents of such notebooks?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were notebooks that were obtained after I left the court and in order to really comment on them I would -- I would like to see the notebooks. Usually there was a date at the beginning and a date at the end, a registration date at the beginning and registration date at the end. When we asked the captain who was responsible for registering the notebooks, the significance of those numbers and the dates, we asked him that as a way to try to gauge the dating of some of the conversations contained within the notebooks to see whether those registration numbers and dates could in some way help date, say, the beginning conversations in the notebook if the operators hadn't recorded the date. And he -- my recollection is that he essentially told us not to rely on the dates that were registered within the notebooks, either at the beginning or at the end.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have indeed shown you a list that was compiled after you had left the Tribunal, but I can also show you a list of the notebooks that you handed over. I'm talking about Prosecutor's exhibit number P1068. Can we please look at page number 4613. Look at number 85, please, for example.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What's the date of this document?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The date is -- maybe we can go back to the first page; 24 April 1998 is the date. And this is the date when you received the collection containing -- containing some 135 or 136 notebooks. And this is the annex with the hand-over document.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So do you need to go to the annex, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, please. I would like to go back to the page that was already shown.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And can you please look at bullet numbers 85 and 86, just to save time, let's not go from one notebook to another. Under 85, can you see that the notebook was registered on the 28th of May, 1995, and that the first entry was made supposedly on the 23rd of April, 1995?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you also look at the following bullet point, number 86. The notebook was registered on the 12th of June, 1995, and the first entry was made on the 10th of April, 1995.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. Yes, I see that. Again, it's hard for me to comment without actually seeing the notebooks because sometimes there were also registration numbers that were indicated at the end of the notebooks. So -- but honestly, we didn't use these registration numbers and dates as a gauge. They were -- we considered them internal working numbers and registration numbers of the ABiH, which didn't affect the analysis of the information contained within the notebooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you for your explanation. Tell me, please, just one more thing. You noticed that in certain places covering the same period of time there were a number of notebooks, there were two or three operators working in two or three places, and there were a number of notebooks that were being used at these two or three places covering the same period of time. Did you notice that, and did you ever wonder about that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were a number of notebooks that were used simultaneously at a specific site, yes, for a specific period of time. That is true. And that was because there were multiple operators working at the time, they all three, or if they were more, couldn't write in one notebook. They needed to have more than one notebook. So they would write in a notebook, each operator, if there were say two or three working at the same time, they would each have a notebook. They would write in it. When one gave the notebook to the typist, maybe someone else was on break, they would pick up another notebook and they would keep writing conversations in that other notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You know that there were a number of notebooks used in parallel, and that in a number of notebooks there were no dates, the dates were not indicated. Could you then conclude, based on that, that there might have been some confusion about the dates, that this could have been a source of confusion?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe that there were any notebooks in which no date was indicated. It's true that in many of the notebooks only a few dates were indicated. So, yes, this was a source of confusion for us early on. At times it was possible to frame conversations by a beginning date and an ending date if the conversations in between the two were consecutive, from day to day to day to day. Once we then received the electronic versions, these helped to solidify the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You received electronic version only a year or a year and a half later?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. That's correct. We -- at the time when we were analysing the material contained in the notebooks, if we were certain of a date, we bolded the date. In our analytical document, in our working document. If we were unsure of a date, if we were guessing at it, we left it unbolded so that we knew whether -- how much certainty we had about the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I wanted to ask you something about the tapes that you have already spoken about. You have told us here that the authorities of Bosnia and Herzegovina in March 1998 allowed you access to these tapes and that there was a total of 19 tapes, as far as I can remember. Could you please explain and tell us whether this access meant that you were allowed to hear those tapes or were you just allowed physical access to those tapes?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wasn't present at the time. I know that the 19 tapes were identified, but I don't -- well, I don't know. I would rather not comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You have also testified about these tapes, and you said that on the 25th of April, 1998, these tapes were transferred to the Tribunal. But they were then returned on the 4th of April, 2000. Can you please tell us who was in charge of those tapes in the meantime, who had custody of the tapes during the -- that period of time?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The tapes were handed over on the 25th of April to Jack Hunter, who took them to Washington, D.C., for analysis and to make copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And he returned them on the 4th of April, 2000, wouldn't that be correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct. He returned the originals on the 4th of April, 2000. I believe that he made copies before that and provided those copies to us before then, which we worked from. But I would have to check the -- the documentation on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And he kept the originals until the 4th of April, and on that date he returned the originals as well, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You were not present at the hand-over of those tapes, were you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to jog your memory by showing you the hand-over record dated 25 April, and I believe that the document was already shown to you by my learned friend on his examination-in-chief. The number of the exhibit is P1069.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I thought you were referring to when the tapes came back to us on the 4th of April of 2000. On the 25th of April, 1998, I was present.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you had an opportunity to read the hand-over document, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can I ask you to look at the penultimate paragraph in the document. In the penultimate paragraph it says that the tapes are being handed over on the 24th of April to the representatives The Hague Tribunal, Jack Hunter is indicated as a member of the American army, and there is a -- a clause here in the joint command of the army of the Federation in the administration for intelligence work and security. At the hand-over of other tapes there should be an inspection and selection of the tapes and the decision should be made on the further use of those tapes. Do you know that after this date, i.e. the 25th of April, 1998, the tapes were listened, selected, and whether a decision was made on the further use of these tapes? Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was -- actually, if I could just make a correction to the translation of Jack Hunter's position first. Oh, it does, in fact, say U.S. Army, though he wasn't with the U.S. Army; he was with ATF, Alcohol Tobacco and Firearms, but that's okay. It's wrong in both documents. No selection was made. The 19 tapes were handed over, we took them all, had copies made, and I returned them, returned copies to the -- to 2 Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, what was agreed on the 25th of April was not followed through, those things that I have just quoted to you were not followed through?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Where you say the tapes should be listened to and selected and the matter of the further use of those tapes should be resolved. Is that what you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes, precisely that.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We had ongoing --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, and it says here that this should be done in the joint command of the Federation army. It says here actually the tapes should be listened to and selected and the matter of the further use of these tapes should be resolved in the joint command of the Federation army. Actually, in its intelligence and security administration.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, I can anticipate what you are saying. Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm going to object to the question because I don't see necessarily that it carries the import that my colleague is -- is implying to the extent that it carries import with respect to the actions of the receiver of the tape as opposed to the actions within the administration of the army, which gives the tape, and I don't think the witness is in a position to answer that question at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. What do you have to state to that, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If the witness cannot reply, she should say so and I will not insist on an answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please look at the paragraph, penultimate paragraph to which you have been referred to earlier on and to which Mr. Zivanovic's question refers. If you wish him to repeat the question he will certainly do so, and tell us whether you are in a position to answer that question. Because obviously it has some relevance, I mean it's ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Could you repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question: Do you know whether the tapes were listened to, as it is indicated here? Were they selected at the intelligence and security administration -- I apologise, I shall rephrase the question. Was the obligation honoured and the obligation was that the Federation army joint command, the intelligence and security administration, the tapes should be listened to and selected and the matter of the further use of these tapes should be resolved. Are you familiar with that? Do you know whether this was followed through, whether this obligation was followed through?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Preliminarily, Your Honour, that seems to be a -- a -- kind of a difficult worded compound question. Secondly, it seems to me that the obligation my colleague is implying exists in that paragraph, it's not clear to whom that obligation applies therefore it doesn't establish a bases upon which the witness can reasonably answer the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop, stop. I think I will leave it. I think the witness is perfectly capable of reading English. She knows exactly what that paragraph says, and Mr. Zivanovic is seeking from her information as to whether all that transpires from that paragraph was adhered to. So you can answer that question, please. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We listened to the tapes. No -- as I -- as I indicated, no selection was made. We received the 19 tapes. We listened to them and we had ongoing contact with the ABiH with regard to the core [phoen] proceedings. I don't have a recollection about whether there was specific communication about the further use of these tapes needing to be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You have just told us that Mr. Hunter took those tapes over on the 25th of April, 1998, and took them to the United States of America, that he had taken over the originals of those tapes. We had different information from the witnesses who were heard before you and who worked with those tapes. There was a testimony by a witness who said that the tapes that were recorded on these two locations were sent to the superior command and that they were re-recorded, that a new recording was made on different tapes, and that the originals were then erased and returned for a repeated use in these two locations, because there was a -- an acute shortage of tapes and this is why this procedure was used. Were you privy to that information as well? Were you aware of that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My -- my problem is, why do you put it to the witness that this information that you have is somewhat different from the information that she gave us? At the end of the day, if you have one tape, and you erase it and you record again, and you erase it and record again, there comes a time when you are left with one recording.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Maybe my question wasn't clear. A witness has told us here in this courtroom, and I'm not going to name the person, that the tapes that were received from these two sites, from these two locations were sent to the command, they were listened to at the command, and certain relevant conversations were recorded on a different tape, whereas the original tapes was erased, the conversations were erased from the original tapes and the -- the empty tapes were -- the tapes were returned to those sites. My question is this: When the witness mentions originals, is she referring to the original originals that were recorded on the sites, or is she referring to the originals which were actually copies of the originals made at the headquarters before the original conversations were erased and the tapes, empty tapes sent back for re-recording.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm referring to the tapes that were given to us by 2 Corps command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And were you told that these were copies of originals or were you told that these were originals? I mean, this is the whole issue.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Right. There were -- and I would have to go back through all 19 tapes to -- and look at them all again, but the one that we're talking about -- I mean, certainly they did record the original conversations on to other tapes, conversations that they considered to be important, that they copied on to other tapes to be archived. I believe that among the 19 tapes that we received there could also have been, but I -- I can't say this for certainty, there could also have been original tapes there. But it is true that there was a shortage of tapes and that they made copies of conversations that they put on to tapes and then sent the used tapes back to the sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. From this follows that the command or superior command of those two sites or two platoons of the corps command had an archive of tapes bearing the recordings of important conversations. Is this what you are saying, if I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The command, being 2 Corps, would have had, could have had compilation tapes, but not the command of the two sites.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And these are the compilation tapes that you received, or did the tapes that you received originate from the two sites?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are these documents being broadcast?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The one on the monitor, I don't think so. Perhaps we can check.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: No, they're are not being broadcasted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: They are not being broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: During your examination-in-chief you heard a tape played back, and you had an opportunity to see a transcript -- the transcript of that conversation. It's P2352A and B. Did you notice or were you informed that the transcript of this tape and the translation of that conversation was not correct in the part?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I can. Before we -- I have the Prosecutor's letter informing me of that, given that I objected to the translation, I believe that it would be practical to take a look at this letter, because it's not a part of the e-court, it can be placed on the ELMO, and to see the -- those inaccuracies in the translation and could you confirm that this is so to me, please? Let's please go to second page. Please, could you place the B/C/S version, not the handwritten copy, because it -- there is -- there are markings and corrections in that part which is -- it is stated that one part from the tape has not been inscribed or transcribed into the notebooks. Could you place the B/C/S version 2352F. Please, let's take a look at the second page of the B/C/S version, and I believe in the English version that is ... Just a moment. I'm not sure whether the corrected version is being put into the e-court system at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have a hard copy, Mr. Zivanovic? Perhaps we can move faster --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I do have this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Usher, could you please help Mr. Zivanovic and put this on the ELMO and move along.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These two documents. Second pages of both documents. Just the second pages of both the B/C/S version and the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I understood Mr. Zivanovic to require the B/C/S version. Yeah. We have both now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exactly to see what was omitted from the original translation of this transcript, I'm not sure whether it's visible clearly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Given that you listened to this tape and you saw a previous version of the transcript, do you agree that those parts were omitted from the previous version?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Does it say here the Popovic and Nikolic are interlocutors? Is it made reference where Popovic says, "Send them" or "A task should be given to them." And were the words to be looked into omitted? Not a correction to be tried and not to be looked into?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The words on the transcript are [B/C/S spoken] [No interpretation]. Right. "To put him to the test," the English translation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me, without those words, which were omitted here, whether Popovic's words could have another meaning?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I don't understand your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You know the content of the conversation.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: If those words were omitted, would his previous utterances be given a different meaning, be interpreted in a different way, if those words, [B/C/S spoken], "ought to be put to the test" were omitted?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't say so, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let's see now. In the previous part of the conversation, the other interlocutor says that those two volunteers would be thrown into the Drina. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I think it says that they would be slaughtered and thrown into the Drina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But it continues with Popovic's words, "Don't do that, send -- give him an assignment." Or it says, "Send them in to attack." So if the words [B/C/S spoken], "be put to a test," were omitted, would Popovic's suggestion that these men be given a task to be put on the attack to be killed, which means that there would not be thrown into the Drina, but would fall to a bullet?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That wasn't the way that I interpreted the conversation.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Without these words?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Excellent. I did not interpret this in this way, but -- either, but this interpretation is much more precise. I am very glad in that you agree with my interpretation, but I do believe that this puts certainly both interlocutors' utterances in a completely different context. Do you agree? These words, [B/C/S spoken], "ought to be put to the test"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye. You first. And then I after.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First, I -- I don't think it's the case that the witness said she agreed with Mr. Zivanovic's interpretation of the meaning of these -- the context, I should say, of the intercept. So I -- I think that's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I meant to --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: -- not an accurate characterisation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Vanderpuye. That's precisely what I wanted to say too. I didn't understand at any time Ms. Frease to concur with your interpretation; rather, she distances herself from it. Correct me if I am wrong, but -- because I mean it will not be the first, nor the last time. But -- but that's how I understood her.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, I must have misunderstood. I will have to ask Ms. Frease to clarify that part to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And shall we do that after the break?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am concurrent with that. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 25 minutes, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you start, Mr. Zivanovic, one moment. All the Defence teams please may I bring to your notice that the Prosecution has earlier on filed submission to convert Witness number 154 to Rule 92 ter witness, and I think it is important to know if there are any objections from any one of you. Yes, Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, we need to look at the testimony before we can decide and know exactly what will be used with the 95 ter, under the Rule 92 ter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: His testimony in Blagojevic, his testimony in Blagojevic. The thing is that this person, should we finish with Ms. Frease before the end of the week, is scheduled to testify on Friday. And it would be in everybody's interests to have the transcripts distributed in time for you to be able to see it, because then we come to the other problem, we haven't had time to read them. So if you could possibly help us here, we will make sure that --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Can we give you an answer in the morning? Or at the beginning of the next session. Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. The other thing is this, Mr. Zivanovic. Excluding our interventions, objections and other problems, but I wouldn't like to classify his objections and our interventions as problems, but you have taken already two hours and 30 minutes. So how much more time do you think you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I will see to it to cut my cross short, but I would like to point out that the question that I broached, I understood for that to be broached by the Prosecution in their examination-in-chief, but this was -- this has now cropped up in interpretation of omissions and corrections so I did not know that this will have to be covered in my cross. I would like to conclude on this issue and then move on to another area, and I will see to it to be as brief as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How much time? We need to know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think I will take 15 to 20 minutes for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We believe you can finish in 10 minutes, Mr. Zivanovic. Go straight to the point --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Ms. Frease, you testified here in connection with these intercepts, or this intercept, and you recall that you listened to the tape?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You read the transcript?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You are fluent in BHS [as interpreted], as you said?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have a good working knowledge of it, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is what I mean. Go straight to the point. You asked her the question already, repeat it. You were under the wrong impression she had agreed with you, she hadn't. So just put the question straight to her. We don't need to repeat whether she has listened to the tape, whether she --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please, my direct question to you, you have words of one interlocutor to the effect that two, those volunteers, will be -- have their throats slit and thrown into the Drina, and the words of the other interlocutor, "No, don't do that. Send them on an attack." Does this imply that the other interlocutor, suggesting that they should be sent to an attack, is suggesting that they would be killed in another manner?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that's not my interpretation of this intercept.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. This is not my interpretation either. I will now move to the other part of what I set out with. I believe that this is sufficient. You said that you analysed the intercepted conversations on the basis of some supporting documents. And by this I mean P1074, tab 8. It goes for an intercepted conversation between Zlatar and Palma, 16th of July, 1995 at 1358?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. May I just remove these documents and have the transcript back up on the screen? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Usher will attend to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please be shown this tab 8, document from tab 8, or under tab 8. In the English version that's -- that's 0603140 in the English version and 06031401 [as interpreted] in the B/C/S version and refers to the supporting documents for the intercept 0603135. I have here 1074, tab 8, as I recorded it. Could I please ask Madam Usher to place this on the ELMO? Could you please place it on the ELMO? I'm not sure it can be seen clearly, particularly the English version.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It can be seen much clearer on e-court. We have the first page or at least one of the pages on -- on e-court. I'm referring to the English version, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please, let's not mention names, but can you tell me whether you see on this document the name of the person who received the fuel in question?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person at the bottom of the document where it says, "Received by."

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I leave that to you, whether you see at any part of the document the name of the person who received the fuel in question.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person to whom the fuel was directed was -- it's indicated here for Lieutenant-Colonel Popovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Excuse me, this is not my question. I asked you whether, on this document, there is any mention of who received and not whom it was sent?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then in the bottom -- at the bottom of the document, box 36, it says, "Received by," and there is a name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we state then that this is not Popovic's name?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you knew or whether through your analysis or through other sources, did you hear that this may be a person who would -- under Popovic's command at the time?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am not familiar with this name.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it known to you that if you take a look at this document, can we state that this fuel was addressed to the command of the Drina Corps? The acronym KDK?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can you scroll up on the document a bit? Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please scroll up.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Box 14 says, "Name and address of recipient." And it says, "Command of --" it has the initials on the original document of KDK, the Command of the Drina Corps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you learn whether the person that you mentioned just a second ago that received the fuel, was that person part of the command of the Drina Corps?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And one correction. If you scroll down to the bottom of the document, please, it doesn't say fuel received by, it means findings and signature of the commission to be received by. And then handwritten, "Received by ...". So we can leave it at that. You have already two answers that he was -- she doesn't know if she was -- he was under the command of Lieutenant-Colonel or whether he was a member of the Drina Corps. Okay. So let's move to the next.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Another question. Can you see from this document where -- into what type of a vehicle was this fuel stored?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The copy that I have is not -- is small and not very clear. It's -- I don't -- I don't see a specific type of vehicle mentioned, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Another question, a whole question, did you stay studying this document for the purposes of the analysis of the relative intercept, or -- or -- or not? I mean was this one of the documents that you examined?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, okay. And did you take into consideration the points that Mr. Zivanovic has raised?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. Not specifically.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the Beara team. You had indicated an hour, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can start off today and we will continue tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good evening, Ms. Frease.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I know it's within been a long day. I'd like to cover a couple of questions with you, specifically in connection with your background. Can you tell me whether or not you are a criminologist?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you an attorney?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No I'm not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you describe for us the experience you had prior to your employment with the OTP which involved handling of evidence in criminal proceedings.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't have any specific such experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about general?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about describing any experience you may have had prior to your employment with the OTP which involved inventorying of evidence?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not inventorying of evidence, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about any experience you may have had prior to your employment with the OTP with respect to chain of custody of potential evidence?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not specifically.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you gave us some opinions, I think, in the last three times that you have testified over the course of the several days, you used some words and I wanted to know what your definitions of it so we can communicate on the same page. You used the word "authentic" a few times, and can you tell us what you mean by the word "authentic"?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: What I mean is whether or not the documents in question are -- come from the source that we believe they come from.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And how about the term "chain of custody" what is your definition of that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Chain of custody describes the point at which material is taken into the custody of the Office of the Prosecutor, and -- and is followed, the integrity of the that custody is followed throughout the period.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get back to that definition a little later, probably tomorrow, but -- so are you saying that the chain of custody and your testimony involving any chain of custody is limited solely to the time that the documents or evidence that we are speaking of, the audio, et cetera, notebooks, that's limited only upon the time that the OTP, its representatives, received it, correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the -- yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Am I fair to understand from your testimony that you have no evidence of what the chain of custody was from the time, for example, these logbooks were written up until the time they were turned over to you in April of 1998?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I -- we don't have -- as far as I know we don't have anything documented about the path that those -- the location of those notebooks from when they were written until they were stored at the site where they were found.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just don't want to lose my computer. If you don't move it every 30 minutes it sometimes -- now, another word that you used yesterday, for my learned friend, on page 68 lines 20 through 25, and page 69, the first -- line 1 through 3, you use the word "material difference" in describing or answering a question of my learned friend. What do you mean by "material difference"?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I try to not use legal terms in general. But what I meant was a -- a difference that would change the -- the overall meaning, I guess, of the -- the substance of the conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What about -- would a material difference be the identity of one of the participants in a purported intercept conversation? Would that be a material difference to you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Why wouldn't it be in any circumstances?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Given the nature of this material, if an intercept operator didn't hear correctly and you had a whole sequence of there being other names used, then it could have been simply that they misheard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, how many alterations or additions or changes in a purported intercept conversation would there need to be in order for you to constitute or confirm that it was a material difference?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't give you a specific answer to that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We'll get some of those tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me talk a little more about your experience while you were here at the OTP. Am I correct in understanding that before the intercept project, I think as you have coined it, you worked in different division or department of the OTP, correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: You were still on this Srebrenica case, correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you were involved in the exhumations of a couple of graves, correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was involved in identifying the locations of graves, but not in the actual exhumations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were you involved during that tenure, and I think it was 1996 through 1997, were you involved at that time in any -- being involved in receiving of any artefacts or potential evidence in a criminal proceeding?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And who were you working under at that time?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we would have to go mission by mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I have two that I wanted to discuss with you, actually, so I will make it simpler. How about the Cerska mission?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The team leader, Jean-Rene Ruez was present during that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And who was the senior forensic advisor, if you recall? William Haglund, do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, could be.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And the other one you were involved with was Pilica, which was Branjevo farm, correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And at that point, could you just describe for us what exactly was your role with respect to the collection and maintenance of artefacts or evidence that you received from those grave sites?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: To backtrack a little bit, on previous missions where we visited other -- other locations, I kept track of material of -- for example blindfolds and other material that we found and logged. During those specific missions -- I would have to see the documents to know whether I was responsible for logging the for example bullet casings that we found.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I know we have a little time. Do you remember that as a result of Dr. Haglund's -- I don't know if I should call it leadership, but his role in these exhumations and your role as being someone involved in that chain of custody and artefacts there was some criticism as to how that was handled. Are you familiar with that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not -- I'm not specifically familiar with any criticism about the Cerska or the Pilica collections, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about any others?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What others?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exhumations, which was something I wasn't involved in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well which ones, do you remember?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember specifically, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this:

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, are you familiar with the 1997 San Antonio report?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have not read the report, but yes, I know ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you know that in that report that they criticise the actual handling of the artefacts?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, by the exhumation teams, but, again, I was not a part of the exhumation teams.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Are you familiar -- and I understand that. Are you familiar with whether or not the committee recommendations that were given after that, in 1997, actually set out what the standard should be for chain of custody in retrieving and keeping potentially criminal evidence such as artefacts?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. If I tell you that in 1997 the committee recommendation was, under number 4, "Develop a standard operating procedure for the collection and handling of evidence." Did anyone share that with you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about under number 10 where it says, "Develop a double 'up down' chain of custody system and form." Did anyone advise you of that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: At any time subsequent to your involvement -- in this first period when you were involved in receiving or inventorying artefacts or criminal evidence, were you ever explained what an up and down chain of custody system was?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: To this day do you know what it is?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: As a result of this report, do you know if any changes were made as to the chain of custody in how the Office of the Prosecutor used and utilised those artefacts?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Artefacts that came from the exhumations?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Could you tell me in the brief moments that we have, what training did you have from anyone at the Office of the Prosecutor as to what the proper system or form was for retaining and preserving criminal evidence in order to satisfy the requirements of any chain of custody?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: This could be a lengthy answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I have all the time in the world.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay, now I think it's working. I am going object to the grounds of vagueness. I don't think that the requirements of any chain of custody sufficiently identifiable for the witness to intelligently respond to the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think I can reply briefly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He is referring to the standards of the OTP.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But, Judge, if I can reply quickly in the minute that we have, her answer indicates she not only can give us a reply, she can give us a rather lengthy one. So I don't know the basis for the objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we will have to come to that tomorrow. Judge Kwon? We finish at 7.00, not a quarter to 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I thought it was a quarter to as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So provided your answer will not take more than 16, 17 minutes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In order to put things in context, in 1995 the war was still going on. In early 1996, March of 1996, we gained access to the territory of Republika Srpska. The Tribunal had been operating for a short period of time at that point. Before going out into the field we were aware that it was necessary to have a system by which to record any evidence that we collected. At the time there was an FBI agent who was working with us, and he was a part of the first missions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: We developed a rudimentary system, tables, and kept track of any evidence, any -- for example, shell casings, identification documents, blindfolds, whatever it was that we found in particular locations. We numbered them, photographed them, and recorded them on these Excel tables. They were brought back to the Court and at the time the Court did not have an evidence locker. Much of the material that we brought back was -- had a foul odour to it. We had no place to store this sort of material, so it was put in a small locker next to the women's dressing -- bathroom on the first floor, which then stunk up the whole first floor. It was after that that we got a container that was put in the back of the building where this material was stored. It was checked into the evidence unit, the evidence unit had control over it, but we were very aware, from the beginning, that there needed to be a process by which we kept track of the material that we were collecting, the sites that we were collecting it from, we had designated letters and numbers -- letter -- letter designations for each site. For example, what is now known as the Orahovac site, we had an LZ designation for Lazete, and numbered the specific items that we found at that location when we visited it. So now I have forgotten your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I just wanted to know what the training you were given from the OTP in order to meet the standards, not only prior to but after the San Antonio 97 report, in connection with the chain of custody.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The training that I received, and the -- the forms that we developed within the OTP really came from the Srebrenica investigation. I am not aware that there -- and there may well have been, but I'm not aware of whether or not there were changes that were made after the 1997 San Antonio report that you refer to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Tell me specifically what consisted of this training that you were given, what did it involve?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It involved sitting down, speaking with the FBI investigator, who had a lot of experience in conducting crime -- crime scene analysis. We had someone else. I don't remember who he worked for at the time, but he also had that type of experience. He was out with us in the field. I received first-hand instruction from them and here before we departed, and made forms that were then used in the field approved by them, in order to ensure that what we did was -- was done in a way that could be tracked and that -- that was responsible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did this -- did this FBI person ever tell you that you should investigate or inquire as -- in order to determine the authenticity of a document to determine where the document was prior to your receipt, who handled it, when they handled it, over what period of time they handled it, and where it was handled?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The FBI agent that I referred to was someone that we worked at -- worked with in the field. So as I said, with bullet casings, identification documents, blindfolds, ligatures, that sort of thing. I believe he had left the -- the court by the time we had worked -- by the time we received the documentary evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So just to help you here, if he didn't, did anyone?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically about handling documents and the need to keep them in their integral, original form, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What about in determining where the documents had come from? Really, that's what I'm looking at. Because as you know, in this instance or in this case, from July 1995 up until April 1998, that's what we think or I think, respectfully, is a critical period to determine where the chain of custody was, terms that you have used, and you have used "authentic", terms that would I like to use with you. What, if anything, did anyone instruct you to make inquiries as a result of you gathering this information for that time period?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one gave me any specific instructions about that period.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What about general instructions?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I said, we had a general idea of where the documents came from by speaking with the people who were responsible for creating those documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's my understanding that you were the person, if I can call you that, in charge of the intercept project. Would that be fair, or was it Mr. Ruez?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not immediately put in charge of the intercept project, but fairly -- within a couple of months I was put in charge of it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Within a couple of months after April of 1998, correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can have 5D187 on the e-court, please. 5D187. And this is -- while they're bringing it up, this is the report from the ATF that you mentioned with Jack L. Hunter. On the top of that report it says, and it's dated the 24th of April, 1998, and it says it is an intermediate report. And my question is to you - you can take a look at that to verify - did you know or did you ever review Mr. Hunter's final report given your testimony here today that he had the logbooks for approximately two years from the end of April 1998 up until April 4th -- 5th, I think you said 2000. Did you ever obtain his final report and what his analysis was of these logbooks and audio tapes, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't believe we ever received a final report from Jack Hunter. He didn't review the logbooks, he only had the tapes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I stand corrected, thank you for clarifying that for me. Do you know if there are any other subsequent reports, after the 24th of April, 1998, that Mr. Hunter provided to the OTP?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Off the top of my head, I don't believe so.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, in sticking with this document, and I know it's getting late, but I think we could cover it in a couple of minutes. If you look at that document, am I correct to understand that this intermediate report discusses the specimens and evidence that was actually collected and that was boxed in relating to a March 11th, 1998 visit, correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I can't see anywhere in that document, although it's four pages long anywhere in that document where it covered that the logbooks were sealed, as you so state?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would make sense because he was specifically addressing the -- the tapes. He wasn't -- he wasn't involved in -- in the logbooks.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So during your visits to the various sites, including the Corps command, as you called it, that would be in Tuzla, right?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. When you visited Tuzla and the various sites, the northern and southern site, is it your testimony that at no time during this visit were logbooks ever discussed or presented to you?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they had been sealed in -- at 2 Corps command in a box, photographs were taken of that box by -- by the people who sealed it, and I believe we may have taken photographs of the box when we opened it in -- in April to check it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. This would have been the visit from March 10th and 11th, 1998, correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We have a trip report from Mr. Hunter dated the 9th through the 14th, 1998, and it's dated March 23rd, 1998. I'll share the ERN number, we don't have it in e-court but I think we can put it on the ELMO, it's ERN number -- just for the record, if I can put that in, 00889127 and 128 at the end. So I know it's late, but if we could just take a quick look at that document. And the ERN number appears right above the word "report" or near that area, but that's irrelevant. Now, if this was the visit with Mr. Hunter, and he mentions the people who were involved, I -- I looked at that and it's a two-page document. Does it mention there at all the logbooks or the notebooks?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Just in the last couple of minutes that we have, I just want to clarify a couple of things. And I know I'm skipping around, so if you don't understand I'll try to put it in context. With respect specifically to the logbooks --

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: -- am I correct that you were not involved in placing the numbers on the front of the logbook with a black pen. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct, for -- for notebooks numbers 1 through 134.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you were the only person who made the notations on those notebooks from the 57 that you received subsequent, so from 135, I think it is, up until the end, correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. To 191, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Who -- who is the person who placed the number or categorised -- or numbered the books 1 through 134, sorry?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe -- I believe it would have been one of two people, and maybe even both people. One of them working for the Office of the Prosecutor at the time, Peter Nicholson, and the other one, the captain --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That we've mentioned that we are not going to identify?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, you also mentioned to us yesterday on page 39 that you did not rely on witnesses' accounts and statements in creating or formulating your analysis respectfully in connection with your testimony. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It's lines 1 through 2, I'm sorry. Just so they have it for the record, page 39.

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: With respect to the authentication binder, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. How about with respect to assessing the reliability?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's correct also, you did not rely on that?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not correct. I did rely on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me just grab your testimony here quickly. And -- and I'll read it to you because I know we have a couple of minutes. It starts on page -- I'm sorry, I actually misspoke on the page. It's actually page 33, lines 20 through 25 and then it goes on to page 34 of yesterday's testimony, lines 1 and 2. So I couldn't read my own handwriting. Here's the question, Ms. Frease, by my learned colleague from the Office of the Prosecutor. Question on line 17: "And in assessing the reliability of the intercepts that are used in this particular case, did you rely exclusively on the corroborative documentary material that you -- that you looked at, or did you rely on other information?" Answer, commencing on line 21, page 33: "On other information as well. The authentication binder was really designed to -- as a sample of the types of -- the type of material that we could draw from in order to independently corroborate some of the intercepts. So in that authentication binder we drew -- I -- at the time I drew from video, from VRS documents, from documents the -- from the RS ministry of the defence ministry, from UNPROFOR. The one big area that I didn't draw from were witness statements." Now, my question to you, is in assessing the reliability, what did you rely on?

utterances.speaker: STEFANIE FREASE [Resumed]
utterances.text: In my view, those are two different questions. The authentication binder was designed as a collection of a few samples of intercepts that could be independently corroborated through other sources. In other words, the authentication of the material. In assessing the reliability of the material -- well, but I guess it also goes to the authentication. In working through the material for the couple of years that I worked on it, I drew from my knowledge of what I knew from the case, and also what I knew from witness testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I could just have one last question, I think it might short circuit something. You mentioned the word or used the words "independently corroborated." In other testimony that I have seen, that I've read, you use the word "internal consistency." Do they mean the same thing to you?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If my colleague could just clarify the context in which the terms were used, I think that would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Shall we do that tomorrow, Mr. --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We'll adjourn until tomorrow afternoon, 2.15. Have a nice evening, all of you.
